content.promptText:
<role>
You are acting as a front-end/UX engineer building a clickable, production-quality prototype — real state and real accessibility, not a static comp.
</role>

<context>
This is the first feature prompt in the sequence, run after the two brand setup fields in the same Claude Design 2.0 session. It must consume the `daybreak-design-system` tokens/components already established, not invent new visual language.
</context>

<instructions>
Prototype a subscription sign-up page for Daybreak (monthly coffee delivery).

Information hierarchy: primary decision first — roast (light / medium / dark), then delivery frequency (weekly / every two weeks / monthly), then bag size — followed by an always-visible price summary and a single primary action, 'Start my subscription'. Keep the price and the CTA visible above the fold on every option combination.

Interaction states to build, not just the happy path:
- Each option control (roast, frequency, bag size) needs a visible selected/unselected state and a keyboard-focus state — build these as real radio groups or equivalent controls, not decorative buttons.
- The price total recomputes immediately on every option change, with no stale or flashing intermediate value.
- The CTA is disabled until a valid combination is selected, with a clear enabled state otherwise.
- Use semantic HTML (fieldset/legend or equivalent grouping for each option set, a real button element for the CTA) so the page is screen-reader navigable.

Responsive behavior: define how the layout collapses on mobile (options and price summary stack vertically; consider a sticky summary on small viewports so price/CTA stay reachable without excessive scrolling).

Make it genuinely clickable — every control responds to a real click/tap, and the price is driven by actual state, not hardcoded per screenshot.

Reason through the information-hierarchy and mobile-layout decisions in `<thinking>` tags first — why roast leads over frequency/size, why a sticky summary is or isn't warranted on mobile — then produce the final prototype.
</instructions>

<done_criteria>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are acting as a motion designer specifying real, implementable motion parameters — not describing a vibe like "smooth."
</role>

<context>
This runs after the wireframe step, in the same chat/session. It adds a choreographed entrance animation to the homepage hero whose layout the wireframe already defined and whose tokens/components the design-system step already established.
</context>

<instructions>
Create an animated hero section for the Daybreak homepage with three sequenced beats: the logo fades in, a bag of coffee slides up from the bottom, and the headline 'Fresh roasted, every month' types onto the screen.

Animate only GPU-cheap properties — `transform` (translate/scale) and `opacity`. This keeps the sequence off the browser's layout/paint path; animating `top`/`left`/`width`/`height` or box-shadow directly forces layout recalculation and reads as jank rather than motion.

- Logo fade-in: opacity 0→1 over ~400–600ms, ease-out (e.g. `cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`) so it decelerates into place rather than fading linearly.
- Coffee bag slide-up: translateY from ~24–40px to 0 combined with opacity 0→1, ~500–700ms, a slightly springy ease-out (e.g. `cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1)`) for a touch of physicality without overshooting into cartoonish bounce.
- Headline type-on: stagger per character or word (~20–40ms stagger step), with total sequence length proportional to headline length rather than a fixed arbitrary duration.
- Sequence the three beats with a deliberate stagger (e.g. logo starts immediately, bag starts ~150–200ms in, headline starts once the bag settles) so it reads as one choreographed entrance rather than three animations firing at once.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` with a genuine fallback — all three elements simply appear via an opacity fade only, no translate/stagger — so the media query changes the actual experience rather than being nominally present.

Reason through the easing-curve choices in `<thinking>` tags first — why an ease-out decelerating curve for the logo versus a springy overshoot curve for the bag, and what emotional effect each is meant to produce — then produce the final implementation.
</instructions>

<example>
One easing-curve spec at the expected level of specificity — every named curve in the deliverable should carry this much information:

`Coffee bag slide-up: translateY 32px→0 + opacity 0→1, 600ms, cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1) (springy ease-out — slight overshoot for physical weight, not a linear or purely decelerating curve).`
</example>

<done_criteria>
- The entrance plays once on load as a single choreographed sequence with no layout jank (only transform/opacity are animated)
- The easing reads as smooth-decelerating rather than linear or excessively bouncy
- The page respects `prefers-reduced-motion` with a genuinely reduced — not identical — fallback
</done_criteria>
install: Run this after the wireframe step, in the same chat/session — it adds motion to the homepage hero the wireframe and design system already define
